Hackers Deploy VIP Keylogger Through Phishing Emails Masquerading as Business Documents

Cyber Security News
2026-05-28 15 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Hackers are using deceptive phishing emails dressed up as routine business documents to spread a dangerous malware strain known as VIP Keylogger. The campaign has been active for months, with attackers showing absolutely no signs of slowing down. VIP Keylogger is part of a broader wave of information-stealing malware that has taken over the threat [&#8230;] The post Hackers Deploy VIP Keylogger Through Phishing Emails Masquerading as Business Documents appeared first on Cyber Security News .

[LLM] VIP Keylogger persistence via UserInitMprLogonScript registry value Installation High
Detects creation or modification of the rarely-used UserInitMprLogonScript registry value, which VIP Keylogger abuses to invoke its PowerShell stager at every user logon. Legitimate use is essentially limited to a small set of enterprise logon-script GPOs and is extremely rare on non-server endpoints. Rationale: The article calls out UserInitMprLogonScript by name as the persistence anchor (STRT explicit recommendation). The key is rarely written outside GPO-pushed logon scripts, making this a high-fidelity, near-zero-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-deploy-vip-keylogger-through-phishing-emails/
ATT&CKT1547.004 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryValueName =~ "UserInitMprLogonScript"
| where isnotempty(RegistryValueData)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryValue =~ "UserInitMprLogonScript"
| where isnotempty(RegistryValueData)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] VIP Keylogger PowerShell stager hidden in INTERNAL_DB_CACHE environment variable Installation High
Hunts for the article-specific registry environment variable INTERNAL_DB_CACHE used by VIP Keylogger to stash an AES-encrypted PowerShell stager, plus any process command-line that subsequently reads it. The string is unique enough to act as a tripwire on its own. Rationale: INTERNAL_DB_CACHE is a unique string named explicitly in the article as the staging variable for the PowerShell stager. Searching it across both registry writes and command-line reads catches both the persistence write and the execution-time read. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-deploy-vip-keylogger-through-phishing-emails/
ATT&CKT1112 T1140 T1027

[LLM] aspnet_compiler.exe making outbound public network connections (VIP Keylogger injection target) Command & Control High
aspnet_compiler.exe is a build-time ASP.NET pre-compilation utility that legitimately has no need to make external network connections. VIP Keylogger injects its final payload into aspnet_compiler.exe; surfacing any public network traffic from that process is high-signal. Rationale: Article explicitly names aspnet_compiler.exe as the injection target. The binary has no legitimate need to reach the public internet (it pre-compiles local ASP.NET sites), so any outbound public connection is essentially TP — particularly to api.telegram.org or vault88x.secure-efficient2.su. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-deploy-vip-keylogger-through-phishing-emails/
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "aspnet_compiler.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("microsoft.com","windowsupdate.com","digicert.com","verisign.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Provider == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 3
| extend Image = tostring(EventData.Image), DestinationIp = tostring(EventData.DestinationIp), DestinationHostname = tostring(EventData.DestinationHostname), DestinationPort = tostring(EventData.DestinationPort), DestinationIsIpv6 = tostring(EventData.DestinationIsIpv6), User = tostring(EventData.User)
| where Image endswith "\\aspnet_compiler.exe"
| where not(DestinationHostname has_any ("microsoft.com","windowsupdate.com"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, User, Image, DestinationIp, DestinationHostname, DestinationPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] VIP Keylogger steganographic PNG payload download from vault88x.secure-efficient2.su Delivery High
Hunts for HTTP(S) fetches of the named steganography PNGs (MSI_105759.png, img_085027.png) or any traffic to the staging host vault88x.secure-efficient2.su. The PNGs carry AES-encoded payload components decoded in-memory by the PowerShell stager. Rationale: vault88x.secure-efficient2.su, MSI_105759.png, and img_085027.png are unique article-cited indicators. The .su TLD plus an oddly-prefixed hostname plus PNG payloads is a tight fingerprint with effectively zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-deploy-vip-keylogger-through-phishing-emails/
ATT&CKT1105 T1027.003 T1071.001

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true

  | where RequestURL has_any ("vault88x.secure-efficient2.su","secure-efficient2.su","MSI_105759.png","img_085027.png") or DestinationHostName has "secure-efficient2.su"

(DnsEvents

[LLM] VIP Keylogger loader chain: script-host parent spawning PowerShell that reads environment variables Installation High
Detects the VIP Keylogger execution pattern where wscript.exe / cscript.exe / cmd.exe (invoked on a .vbs/.js/.bat attachment) spawns PowerShell that reads its stager from a registry/environment variable. This is the bridge between the document-themed lure and the encoded stager. Rationale: Combines the article's three diagnostic elements: (1) script-host parent invoking a .vbs/.js/.bat, (2) PowerShell child, (3) command-line referencing an environment variable read (or the literal INTERNAL_DB_CACHE name). Each alone is noisy; together they isolate the VIP Keylogger loader chain. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-deploy-vip-keylogger-through-phishing-emails/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("$env:","[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable","gci env:","Get-ChildItem env:","INTERNAL_DB_CACHE")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".js",".bat",".vbe",".jse")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentName = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1]), ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where tolower(ParentName) in ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe")
| where tolower(ChildName) in ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("$env:","[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable","gci env:","Get-ChildItem env:","INTERNAL_DB_CACHE")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Script Host Spawning PowerShell Reading Environment Variable (VIP Keylogger)
id: 2f9c4a18-8d62-4b3f-91c2-3e1a5f0d8e72
description: VIP Keylogger loader pattern - wscript/cscript/cmd invokes PowerShell that reads its stager from a registry environment variable (INTERNAL_DB_CACHE).
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-deploy-vip-keylogger-through-phishing-emails/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28

  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_env:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '$env:'
      - '[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable'
      - 'gci env:'
      - 'Get-ChildItem env:'
      - 'INTERNAL_DB_CACHE'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_env
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:*\\wscript.exe OR @ParentImage:*\\cscript.exe OR @ParentImage:*\\cmd.exe OR @ParentImage:*\\WScript.exe OR @ParentImage:*\\CScript.exe) (@Image:*\\powershell.exe OR @Image:*\\pwsh.exe OR @Image:*\\PowerShell.exe) (@CommandLine:*$env:* OR @CommandLine:*GetEnvironmentVariable* OR @CommandLine:*INTERNAL_DB_CACHE*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript|cmd)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\$env:|GetEnvironmentVariable|Get-ChildItem env:|gci env:|INTERNAL_DB_CACHE)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

[LLM] VIP Keylogger sandbox / geolocation reconnaissance via reallyfreegeoip and checkip.dyndns from non-browser process Actions on Objectives High
Surfaces requests to reallyfreegeoip.org/xml/ or checkip.dyndns.org made by interpreters or LOLBins rather than browsers. VIP Keylogger uses these endpoints for IP-based sandbox detection and host geolocation before fully unpacking. Rationale: Both URLs are explicitly cited as VIP Keylogger sandbox/geolocation checks. Real users hit these only via browsers (and rarely even then); a script interpreter or aspnet_compiler.exe resolving them is a near-pure TP. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-deploy-vip-keylogger-through-phishing-emails/
ATT&CKT1016 T1016.001 T1497.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("reallyfreegeoip.org/xml","checkip.dyndns.org") or RemoteUrl endswith "reallyfreegeoip.org" or RemoteUrl endswith "checkip.dyndns.org"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","safari.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Name has_any ("reallyfreegeoip.org","checkip.dyndns.org")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has_any ("reallyfreegeoip.org/xml","checkip.dyndns.org") or DestinationHostName in~ ("reallyfreegeoip.org","checkip.dyndns.org")
  | where not(RequestClientApplication has_any ("Chrome","Edg/","Firefox","Safari"))
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

let BadHashes = dynamic(["95e6c6c13f65217f41c371abf6d03594b2bfed2259a1813bb4222fb2d3c32745", "07ee41817b9f338719bea03676ab607349cc3accba0dddb800f6276a01cfdd9f", "2df582bb41d1e6f0a6d44e8dbc1d8bca8e3d332bb268685b9dfc381a566c63a6", "8d1f59c65ebe64d0e817ffe7ecbf1d5a4bc3768d896c934b00dfd57263c3fe15", "8d5de337baa0b0938e4283324d3b1e8ccbdeed694aab3b6118910476200c621b", "14b25dfcc6e7f69992b3f5543bcc9ebe86bd0b682e211f49cb62c019d8e9bc4d", "28613bfb4e866186133235a88e318df3059b01001f297ad6a524eab0885305a5", "d2ab8dcab70822c839912cb672e93de459e5608bea210c78a1be56b54cbd8f81", "9bca7a3ac404807c63670141a3459eac24450e0cffbe1066cd3c8b503a917170", "9905c76ccf4ebdd12e1df63047a3206026073781d885165e82d298656b5f4937", "927c6d68f6413e437e4a919b2007f6a2ade32be71f80467856ce19a0325b63eb", "ae6918bfe8774e1ec1ec34f3db26e7e548dd0dc33a4e6fa80970e0bd2ba7ad9d", "a2862e4d2c722c7bfc86aa6c2c589455659b7a4ce6bb15ae55706df40e0f1f4e", "cbdecb69250504d0b00bf3a9ac2209e3f6000553aa0e8980489b8d88106af6b7", "b79d5ad4a4b03f9b153d27d356c6e62648fa87c2c378af407b894ed66119b921", "2801ccd00ad4c93afcc23b9f8e5f56a8ddef81c1f4b331978d9b288a69f8ce4d", "93cca0789e92ef11ccc9abd411bdc621a34138aaee4db3241f5266bccc7eac78"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClearFake Uses BSC Testnet Smart Contracts for Takedown-Resistant Command and Control

Cyber Security News
2026-05-28 18 use cases 10 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new and dangerously clever malware campaign called ClearFake has been caught using blockchain smart contracts to run its operations, making it nearly impossible for security teams to shut it down. Instead of relying on traditional servers that can be taken offline, the attackers hid their command-and-control infrastructure inside the BNB Smart Chain testnet, a [&#8230;] The post ClearFake Uses BSC Testnet Smart Contracts for Takedown-Resistant Command and Control appeared first on Cyber Security News .

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1027 T1190 T1204.002 T1204.004 T1218.011 T1486 T1555.003 T1566 T1574.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ClickFix Run-dialog rundll32 with WebDAV UNC port syntax · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ClearFake Uses BSC Testnet Smart Contracts for Takedown-Resistant Command and Co
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rundll32 loads put34b.camp DLL via WebDAV mini-redirector · [LLM] ClearFake Python RAT staging in FileZilla Data masquerade directory
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ClearFake C2 query to BNB Smart Chain testnet RPC endpoint · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ClearFake dllhost spawned by rundll32 injecting into Chrome/Edge · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] ClearFake C2 query to BNB Smart Chain testnet RPC endpoint Command & Control High
Detects browser or any endpoint process performing a JSON-RPC query to bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com — the Stage 1 ClearFake EtherHiding lookup that fetches the on-chain Stage 2 JavaScript from Smart Contract A before the ClickFix overlay renders. No legitimate enterprise application routinely contacts BSC testnet RPC. Rationale: Pivots on the single named RPC endpoint the article explicitly recommends blocking (bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com) — the chain breaks here before any payload runs. Corroborated by Trend Micro vendor write-up (trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html) and gbhackers coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://gbhackers.com/clearfake-abuses-bsc-testnet/ • https://www.vmray.com/threat-intelligence-insights-pivoting-off-the-blockchain/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com"
   or (RemoteUrl has "publicnode.com" and RemoteUrl has "bsc-testnet")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          User = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| union (
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where HttpHostName has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com" or Url has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, EventProduct
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/bsc-testnet-rpc\.publicnode\.com/i

[LLM] ClickFix Run-dialog rundll32 with WebDAV UNC port syntax Exploitation High
Detects rundll32.exe launched directly from explorer.exe (Run dialog paste) with a UNC path embedding the @80 / @443 WebDAV mini-redirector syntax — the exact ClickFix execution shape Trend Micro recorded for the ClearFake Windows payload that pulls put34b.camp into memory. Rationale: Combines three article-specific signals: parent explorer.exe (Run dialog), child rundll32.exe, and the exact WebDAV UNC `\\host@port\` syntax or literal put34b.camp filename. The triple combination has near-zero benign baseline; explorer→rundll32 alone is high-FP, the UNC port syntax disambiguates. Cross-checked with gbhackers ClickFix-WebDAV writeup and Trend Micro report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://gbhackers.com/rundll32-and-webdav/ • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/the-clickfix-evolution-new-variant-replaces-powershell-with-rundll32-and-webdav/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1059 T1204.004 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\\\[^\\]+@(80|443|8080)\\"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "put34b.camp"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\\\[^\\]+@\d+\\.+,#1\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\rundll32.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\explorer.exe"

[LLM] Rundll32 loads put34b.camp DLL via WebDAV mini-redirector Installation High
Detects the actual in-memory load of the ClearFake stage payload — the file named put34b.camp loaded by rundll32.exe — and the WebClient (svchost) outbound HTTP fetch that retrieves it. Fires even if the Run-dialog parent chain is obscured. Rationale: put34b.camp is a campaign-specific filename named verbatim in the article's IoC table, with no benign WebDAV use case. Combining DLL image-load by rundll32 + WebClient svchost fetch gives both the local effect and the wire-layer corroboration. Cross-referenced with Trend Micro and ASR/WebDAV reporting (lindensec.com). Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://www.lindensec.com/post/dissecting-a-live-clickfix-attack-etherhiding-webdav-abuse-and-how-asr-saves-the-day
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let LoadEvents = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "put34b.camp" or FolderPath has "put34b.camp"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId;
let WebDavFetch = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("WebClient","WebDav","DavSetCookie")
    | where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
LoadEvents
| union WebDavFetch
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "put34b.camp" or TargetFilePath has "put34b.camp"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| union (
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SrcUsername != "" and DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8080)
    | where NetworkApplicationProtocol in~ ("http","https")
    | where Url has "put34b.camp" or DstHostname has "put34b.camp"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:7 AND @Image:(*\\rundll32.exe OR *\\Rundll32.exe OR *\\RUNDLL32.EXE) AND (@ImageLoaded:*put34b.camp* OR @ImageLoaded:*PUT34B.CAMP*)

[LLM] ClearFake dllhost spawned by rundll32 injecting into Chrome/Edge Actions on Objectives High
Detects the post-exploitation chain where rundll32.exe spawns dllhost.exe which then injects remote threads into chrome.exe and msedge.exe to harvest browser sessions, cookies, and saved credentials (SectopRAT / ACRStealer behaviour confirmed in Trend Micro execution profiles). Rationale: dllhost.exe legitimately runs only as a COM surrogate and always carries the `/Processid:{...}` GUID. A dllhost.exe without that switch and parented to rundll32.exe is highly anomalous — Trend Micro's execution profile (Figure 7) shows this exact tree leading to chrome.exe / msedge.exe credential theft. Excluding the legitimate CLSID-arg form keeps FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://blog.vega.io/posts/clickfix_sectoprat_campaign/
ATT&CKT1055.002 T1055.003 T1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let SuspiciousDllHost = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
    | where FileName =~ "dllhost.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine !has "/Processid:{"   // legitimate dllhost has COM CLSID
    | project DllHostTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
              DllHostPid = ProcessId, ParentPid = InitiatingProcessId,
              ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let RemoteThreadInjection = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","ProcessInjectionDetected","AsyncRpcThreadCreated")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dllhost.exe"
    | where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","firefox.exe")
    | project InjectionTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
              InjectorPid = InitiatingProcessId, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType;
SuspiciousDllHost
| join kind=inner RemoteThreadInjection on DeviceId
| where InjectionTime between (DllHostTime .. DllHostTime + 5m)
| project DllHostTime, InjectionTime, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd, DllHostPid, TargetProcess, ActionType
| order by DllHostTime desc
let SuspiciousDllHost = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName endswith @"\rundll32.exe"
    | where ActingProcessName endswith @"\dllhost.exe"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "/Processid:{"
    | project DllHostTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname,
              ActorUsername, ActingProcessId, ParentProcessCommandLine;
SuspiciousDllHost
source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:1 AND @ParentImage:(*\\rundll32.exe OR *\\Rundll32.exe OR *\\RUNDLL32.EXE) AND @Image:(*\\dllhost.exe OR *\\Dllhost.exe OR *\\DLLHOST.EXE) AND -@CommandLine:"/Processid:{*"
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\dllhost\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/rundll32\.exe/i
| NOT regex("/Processid:\\{", field=CommandLine)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, TargetImageFileName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp)])

[LLM] ClearFake Python RAT staging in FileZilla Data masquerade directory Installation High
Detects dllhost.exe (or any non-FileZilla process) writing pythonw.exe / helper.py / libvlccore.dll / remote_debugging.pyd into a FileZilla Data subdirectory — the ClearFake masquerade location for the Python-based RAT and ACRStealer DLL sideload triad described in Trend Micro's Figure 8. Rationale: Four named filenames + FileZilla folder + a non-FileZilla writer is a near-zero baseline shape. The article calls the FileZilla Data directory out explicitly as the masquerade target (Figure 8), and libvlccore.dll is reused for the VLC DLL-sideload triad — both highly campaign-specific. Cross-checked with Vega.io ClickFix-SectopRAT analysis and Trend Micro report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://blog.vega.io/posts/clickfix_sectoprat_campaign/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1574.001 T1059.006 T1105

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","helper.py","libvlccore.dll","remote_debugging.pyd")
| where FolderPath has "FileZilla"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("FileZilla.exe","filezilla.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe","FileZilla_3*.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          User = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          DroppedFile = FileName,
          FolderPath,
          SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","helper.py","libvlccore.dll","remote_debugging.pyd")
| where TargetFilePath has "FileZilla"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith @"\FileZilla.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\msiexec.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: |

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase

    selection_parent:

Medium

New Linux CIFSwitch Kernel Vulnerability Allows Attackers to Gain Root Access

Cyber Security News
2026-05-28 7 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A newly disclosed Linux local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerability dubbed &#8220;CIFSwitch&#8221; enables low-privileged users to gain root access by abusing a logic flaw between the Linux kernel CIFS client and the userspace&#160;cifs-utils&#160;package. The bug was discovered by security researcher&#160;Asim Manizada, who has published a detailed technical write-up and PoC to help defenders assess their exposure [&#8230;] The post New Linux CIFSwitch Kernel Vulnerability Allows Attackers to Gain Root Access appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Unprivileged user creates rogue nsswitch.conf or libnss_*.so.2 in writable namespace stage dir
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] cifs.upcall loading libnss_*.so.2 from non-system path — CIFSwitch namespace switch
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] cifs.upcall (root helper) writing to /etc/sudoers.d — CIFSwitch PoC payload · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New Linux CIFSwitch Kernel Vulnerability Allows Attackers to Gain Root Access
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] cifs.upcall (root helper) writing to /etc/sudoers.d — CIFSwitch PoC payload Installation High
Detects the privilege-escalation payload from the CIFSwitch (cifs.spnego) exploit: cifs.upcall executes as root, switches into the attacker's mount namespace, and the rogue libnss_*.so.2 it loads writes a sudoers entry granting the attacker root. cifs.upcall has no legitimate reason to touch /etc/sudoers.d. Rationale: Cross-checked with Asim Manizada's write-up (heyitsas.im/posts/cifswitch) and the oss-security post — both confirm the PoC's NSS module drops an /etc/sudoers.d entry as the root primitive. cifs.upcall touching sudoers.d has effectively zero legitimate baseline, making this a high-fidelity exploit signature rather than a generic sudo-tamper rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/05/28/2 • https://heyitsas.im/posts/cifswitch/
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cifs.upcall"
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "cifs.upcall"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in ("auth","authpriv","kern","user")
| where ProcessName =~ "cifs.upcall" or SyslogMessage has "cifs.upcall"
| where SyslogMessage has "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] cifs.upcall loading libnss_*.so.2 from non-system path — CIFSwitch namespace switch Exploitation High
Detects the core CIFSwitch exploit primitive: cifs.upcall runs as root, switches into the attacker's mount namespace, and loads a libnss_*.so.2 from an attacker-controlled location instead of /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, /usr/lib, or /usr/lib64. Any libnss image load by cifs.upcall outside system library paths is anomalous. Rationale: Per the Manizada write-up (heyitsas.im) and oss-security disclosure, the exploit primitive is namespace-confused root NSS lookup pulling libnss_*.so.2 from the attacker's mount namespace. Restricting the load source to non-system paths catches the exploit while suppressing every legitimate cifs.upcall Kerberos auth, where libnss is loaded from /lib or /usr/lib only. Cross-checked against: • https://heyitsas.im/posts/cifswitch/ • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/05/28/2
ATT&CKT1574.006 T1068 T1611

| where not (FolderPath startswith "/lib/"
          or FolderPath startswith "/lib64/"
          or FolderPath startswith "/usr/lib/"
          or FolderPath startswith "/usr/lib64/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

title: cifs.upcall loads libnss_*.so.2 from non-system path (CIFSwitch exploit)
id: 4b7a2d11-2c5f-4f6a-9c1d-3a1f9d7e2a02
description: The CIFSwitch exploit forces cifs.upcall (running as root) into an attacker mount namespace where a rogue libnss_*.so.2 outside the system library directories is loaded during the NSS account lookup. Detects that image load.
references:

[LLM] Unprivileged user creates rogue nsswitch.conf or libnss_*.so.2 in writable namespace stage dir Weaponization Medium
Hunts the exploit preparation phase: before triggering request_key(cifs.spnego), the attacker plants a fake /etc/nsswitch.conf and malicious libnss_*.so.2 inside a directory that will become the root of their unprivileged mount namespace (typically /tmp/<rand>/etc/, /dev/shm/, or a chroot under their HOME). Targeting these file drops gives lead-time before privesc. Rationale: Manizada's write-up describes planting a rogue /etc/nsswitch.conf + libnss_*.so.2 inside an attacker-controlled mount namespace; before unshare(2)/mount(2), those files have to exist somewhere writable by the unprivileged user. Combining filename pattern + writable-dir + non-package-manager writer catches the staging step regardless of the exact namespace-trigger binary used. Hunting tier because tmp file writes have FP weight — pairs naturally with UC1/UC2 as a leading indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://heyitsas.im/posts/cifswitch/ • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/05/28/2

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3da1fdf4efbc490041eb4f836bf596201203f8f2") or SHA1 in~ ("3da1fdf4efbc490041eb4f836bf596201203f8f2") or MD5 in~ ("3da1fdf4efbc490041eb4f836bf596201203f8f2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3da1fdf4efbc490041eb4f836bf596201203f8f2") or SHA1 in~ ("3da1fdf4efbc490041eb4f836bf596201203f8f2") or MD5 in~ ("3da1fdf4efbc490041eb4f836bf596201203f8f2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3da1fdf4efbc490041eb4f836bf596201203f8f2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
