title: Python Interpreter Spawning Shell with os.system Indicator (Zapocalypse)
id: 9d2b1f48-7c0a-4e1a-b9e2-2af3b8e1d6a1
description: Detects Python interpreters spawning Unix shells with command lines referencing os.system, subprocess primitives, or /proc/self/mem — the sandbox-escape pattern from the Zapocalypse exploit chain against Code by Zapier.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/zapocalypse-attack-chain-zapier/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|re: '/python[0-9.]*$'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/ash'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'os.system'
      - 'subprocess.Popen'
      - 'subprocess.call'
      - 'subprocess.run'
      - '/proc/self/mem'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:(python OR python3 OR python3.9 OR python3.10 OR python3.11) @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash) (@process.command_line:*os.system* OR @process.command_line:*subprocess* OR @process.command_line:*"/proc/self/mem"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^python[0-9.]*$/i ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|ash)$/i
| CommandLine=/(os\.system|subprocess\.(Popen|call|run)|\/proc\/self\/mem)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
| sort(count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_cmdline from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.9","python3.10","python3.11") Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","ash") (Processes.process="*os.system*" OR Processes.parent_process="*os.system*" OR Processes.process="*subprocess*" OR Processes.process="*/proc/self/mem*") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where host="*lambda*" OR host="*container*" OR host="*ecs*" OR host="*runner*"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_cmdline from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.9","python3.10","python3.11") Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","ash") (Processes.process="*os.system*" OR Processes.parent_process="*os.system*" OR Processes.process="*subprocess*" OR Processes.process="*/proc/self/mem*") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where host="*lambda*" OR host="*container*" OR host="*ecs*" OR host="*runner*"
[LLM] Process reading /proc/self/mem or /proc/<pid>/mem on Linux container host (Zapocalypse stage 2) Installation High
Hunts for processes that open /proc/self/mem or /proc/<pid>/mem — the exact primitive Token Security used to recover STS tokens orphaned in Lambda heap after del os.environ[k] cleanup. Legitimate readers are essentially debuggers (gdb/strace) and a handful of perf tools; everything else is anomalous. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim string `/proc/self/mem` (article code block 2) and the article's explicit claim that del os.environ[k] does not wipe the heap. Legitimate /proc/<pid>/mem readers on a production server are essentially gdb/strace/perf — anything else is anomalous and matches MITRE T1003.007. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/007/ • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileAccessed","FileOpened")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"^/proc/(self|[0-9]+)/mem$"
   or FileName == "mem" and FolderPath startswith "/proc/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gdb","strace","ltrace","perf","crash","systemd-coredump","abrt-hook-ccpp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in ("kern","user","authpriv","daemon")
| where SyslogMessage has "/proc/self/mem" or SyslogMessage has "/mem" and SyslogMessage has "/proc/"
| where SyslogMessage !has "gdb" and SyslogMessage !has "strace" and SyslogMessage !has "systemd-coredump"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage, Facility
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Suspicious Read of /proc/self/mem or /proc/<pid>/mem (Credential Scrape)
id: 4f8e2c91-6b3d-4a8e-9f7c-1e4d2b7a8f93
description: Detects non-debugger processes opening /proc/self/mem or /proc/<pid>/mem — the credential-recovery primitive from the Zapocalypse exploit chain against Zapier's Code-by-Zapier Lambda runtime. Used to scrape STS tokens orphaned in process heap after env-var cleanup.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/zapocalypse-attack-chain-zapier/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.t1003.007
  - attack.t1552.001
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|re: '^/proc/(self|[0-9]+)/mem$'
  filter_debuggers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/gdb'
      - '/strace'
      - '/ltrace'
      - '/perf'
      - '/systemd-coredump'
  condition: selection and not filter_debuggers
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(SYSCALL OR PATH) (@file.path:"/proc/self/mem" OR @file.path:/proc/*/mem) -@process.executable.path:(*/gdb OR */strace OR */ltrace OR */perf OR */systemd-coredump)
#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|ProcessRollup2)$/
| (TargetFileName=/^\/proc\/(self|\d+)\/mem$/ OR CommandLine=/\/proc\/(self|\d+)\/mem/)
| NOT ImageFileName=/\/(gdb|strace|ltrace|perf|systemd-coredump)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, TargetFileName], function=count())
| sort(count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.process) as cmdline from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path IN ("/proc/self/mem","/proc/*/mem") by host Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search NOT proc IN ("gdb","strace","ltrace","perf","crash","systemd-coredump")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.process) as cmdline from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path IN ("/proc/self/mem","/proc/*/mem") by host Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search NOT proc IN ("gdb","strace","ltrace","perf","crash","systemd-coredump")
[LLM] ECR enumeration + image layer pull chain from Lambda execution role (Zapocalypse stage 3) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts CloudTrail for the exact ECR API quartet — DescribeRepositories, ListImages, BatchGetImage, GetDownloadUrlForLayer — performed by an AssumedRole session within a short window. This is the literal lateral-movement sequence the researchers ran via the misconfigured allow_nothing_role. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim API names from Table 1 Row 3: DescribeRepositories, ListImages, BatchGetImage, GetDownloadUrlForLayer. Cross-checked against MITRE T1526 (Cloud Service Discovery) and AWS ECR API reference — these four together in a 15-minute window from an assumed role indicate enumeration intent, not normal pull-image traffic from ECS/EKS (which uses a much narrower call pattern centered on BatchGetImage + GetDownloadUrlForLayer for known repos). Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/APIReference/Welcome.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1526/
ATT&CKT1526 T1078.004 T1213.003
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType in ("DescribeRepositories","ListImages","BatchGetImage","GetDownloadUrlForLayer")
| extend RoleArn = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).userIdentity.arn)
| extend RoleName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName)
| extend UserType = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).userIdentity.type)
| where UserType == "AssumedRole"
| summarize ApiCalls = make_set(ActionType), CallCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RoleName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 15m)
| where array_length(ApiCalls) >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventSource == "ecr.amazonaws.com"
| where EventName in ("DescribeRepositories","ListImages","BatchGetImage","GetDownloadUrlForLayer")
| where UserIdentityType == "AssumedRole"
| summarize ApiCalls = make_set(EventName), CallCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SourceIPs = make_set(SourceIpAddress) by SessionIssuerUserName = tostring(parse_json(UserIdentitySessionContext).sessionIssuer.userName), bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where array_length(ApiCalls) >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(DescribeRepositories OR ListImages OR BatchGetImage OR GetDownloadUrlForLayer) @userIdentity.type:AssumedRole
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, userIdentity.type, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent
| filter eventSource = "ecr.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["DescribeRepositories","ListImages","BatchGetImage","GetDownloadUrlForLayer"]
      and userIdentity.type = "AssumedRole"
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| stats count() as calls, count_distinct(eventName) as distinct_apis, earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen, latest(@timestamp) as last_seen by userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress
| filter distinct_apis >= 3
| sort calls desc
CLOUD
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Changes.command) as apis values(All_Changes.src) as src values(All_Changes.user) as user from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category="cloud" All_Changes.command IN ("DescribeRepositories","ListImages","BatchGetImage","GetDownloadUrlForLayer") by All_Changes.user_type All_Changes.user_name span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | eval distinct_apis=mvcount(apis) | where distinct_apis >= 3 AND user_type="AssumedRole"
[LLM] AssumedRole STS-derived call from Lambda role used outside Lambda service IP space (Zapocalypse stage 3 pivot) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CloudTrail for API calls made under an AssumedRole session whose role is normally only assumed by AWS Lambda (lambda.amazonaws.com), but where the call's sourceIPAddress is not the Lambda service identifier or expected NAT egress. This is how the recovered STS tokens get used outside the Lambda sandbox after Zapocalypse Stage 2. Rationale: Anchors on the article's claim that the recovered STS token was used outside the Lambda sandbox to enumerate ECR — i.e. the role's session principal was used from a non-Lambda source IP / user-agent. The role-naming heuristic (allow_nothing_role suffix `_role`, `*lambda*`, `*function*`) is taken directly from the article's mention of the role's literal name. Cross-checked against MITRE T1550.001 (Application Access Token). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/001/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/cloudtrail-integration.html
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| extend RawJson = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend UserType = tostring(RawJson.userIdentity.type)
| extend SessionIssuerName = tostring(RawJson.userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName)
| extend SessionIssuerType = tostring(RawJson.userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.type)
| extend ClientUserAgent = tostring(RawJson.userAgent)
| extend SrcIp = tostring(RawJson.sourceIPAddress)
| where UserType == "AssumedRole"
| where SessionIssuerType == "Role"
| where SessionIssuerName has_any ("lambda","function","serverless")
   or SessionIssuerName endswith "_role"
| where SrcIp != "AWS Internal" and SrcIp !endswith ".amazonaws.com"
| where ClientUserAgent !has "Lambda" and ClientUserAgent !has "aws-internal"
| project Timestamp, SessionIssuerName, ActionType, SrcIp, ClientUserAgent, RawJson
| order by Timestamp desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where UserIdentityType == "AssumedRole"
| extend SessionIssuerName = tostring(parse_json(UserIdentitySessionContext).sessionIssuer.userName)
| extend SessionIssuerType = tostring(parse_json(UserIdentitySessionContext).sessionIssuer.type)
| where SessionIssuerType == "Role"
| where SessionIssuerName has_any ("lambda","function","serverless") or SessionIssuerName endswith "_role"
| where SourceIpAddress != "AWS Internal"
| where SourceIpAddress !endswith ".amazonaws.com"
| where UserAgent !has "Lambda" and UserAgent !has "aws-internal"
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, EventSource, SessionIssuerName, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent, AWSRegion
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:cloudtrail @userIdentity.type:AssumedRole (@userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName:*lambda* OR @userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName:*function* OR @userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName:*_role) -@useragent:*Lambda* -@network.client.ip:"AWS Internal"
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, userIdentity.type, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.type, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, awsRegion
| filter userIdentity.type = "AssumedRole"
      and userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.type = "Role"
      and (userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName like /(?i)lambda/ or userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName like /(?i)function/ or userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName like /_role$/)
      and sourceIPAddress != "AWS Internal"
      and not (sourceIPAddress like /amazonaws\.com$/)
      and not (userAgent like /Lambda/)
      and not (userAgent like /aws-internal/)
| stats count() as calls, count_distinct(eventName) as distinct_apis, count_distinct(sourceIPAddress) as distinct_ips by userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress
| sort calls desc
CLOUD
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Changes.command) as apis values(All_Changes.src) as src from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category="cloud" All_Changes.user_type="AssumedRole" by All_Changes.user_name All_Changes.src All_Changes.user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | search user_name="*lambda*" OR user_name="*function*" | search NOT user_agent="*Lambda*" AND NOT src="AWS Internal" AND NOT src="lambda.amazonaws.com"
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gogs RCE: git rebase invoked with --exec flag (argument injection)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Post-exploit shell or LOLBin spawned by git invoked from Gogs server
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Gogs RCE: git rebase invoked with --exec flag (argument injection) Exploitation High
Detects the Gogs zero-day argument-injection RCE in flight: the Gogs server process invokes 'git rebase' with an attacker-controlled branch name that smuggles a '--exec=' flag, causing arbitrary command execution as the Gogs user. The smoking gun is a 'git rebase' process whose command line contains '--exec' (or '-x') and whose parent is the gogs binary. Rationale: The article explicitly names the injected flag ('--exec') and the abused command path ('git rebase' during 'Rebase before merging'), with the Gogs server as the parent that invokes git. A 'git rebase' process whose parent is gogs and whose argv contains '--exec' has effectively no legitimate use — the Gogs codebase never legitimately passes --exec to rebase. Cross-referenced with Rapid7's earlier Gogs argument-injection family (CVE-2024-39930/39932/39933) which the article explicitly compares this flaw to. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/securing-developer-tools-unpatched-code-vulnerabilities-in-gogs-1 • https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/securing-developer-tools-unpatched-code-vulnerabilities-in-gogs-2 • https://thehackernews.com/2024/07/critical-vulnerabilities-disclosed-in.html • https://github.com/gogs/gogs/issues/7777

[LLM] Post-exploit shell or LOLBin spawned by git invoked from Gogs server Installation High
Follow-on detection for the Gogs --exec argument injection: once 'git rebase --exec=<cmd>' fires, git executes the attacker's command, producing a process tree of gogs -> git -> /bin/sh|bash|curl|wget|nc|python. Hunts for any non-git child of a git process whose parent is the Gogs server binary — the post-exploitation footprint the article describes ('compromise the server, dump credentials, pivot'). Rationale: The article enumerates the post-exploit objectives explicitly — 'compromise the server, read every repository on the instance, dump credentials (password hashes, API tokens, SSH keys, 2FA secrets), pivot to other network-accessible systems'. Git itself has zero legitimate reason to spawn shells, network tools, or interpreters; in the Gogs server context, git only invokes other git plumbing binaries. Any non-git child of git on a Gogs host is the --exec payload landing. Confirmed pattern matches Rapid7's documented Gogs argument-injection family (CVE-2024-39930/39932/39933). Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/securing-developer-tools-unpatched-code-vulnerabilities-in-gogs-1 • https://thehackernews.com/2024/07/critical-vulnerabilities-disclosed-in.html • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/attackers-exploited-gogs-zero-day-months

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] wscript/cscript executing .js extracted from archive utility (WinRAR/7zip/Explorer ZIP) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JS backdoor C2 callback to aryamint/talruit/mpwirerope/ethara on non-standard ports · [LLM] JS backdoor C2 traffic with outdated MSIE user-agent on non-standard ports · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] JS backdoor C2 callback to aryamint/talruit/mpwirerope/ethara on non-standard ports Command & Control High
Hunts outbound connections from script-host processes (wscript/cscript/mshta) to the Intrinsec-published C2 infrastructure (aryamint.com, scan.aryamint.com) and spam-relay domains (talruit.com, mail.talruit.com, mpwirerope.com, ethara.org) or hard IPs 91.92.243.79 / 158.94.211.76 / 83.142.209.64, with bias toward the campaign's distinctive ports 2002, 2004, 7273. Combining a script-host parent with a known-bad destination is article-specific and high-fidelity. Rationale: Pivot uses the article's explicit IOC table (3 IPs, 6 domains, 3 distinctive non-standard ports 2002/2004/7273) combined with a script-host parent — the cmd-line/binary names Intrinsec named (.js delivered via wscript). Cross-checked Intrinsec primary report and Spamhaus listings for AS205759/AS202412; specific IOCs remain single-source so confidence rests on the narrow string match, not the broader actor attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.intrinsec.com/en/pivoting-on-a-malspam-infrastructure-delivering-js-malware-backed-by-bulletproof-networks/ • https://intel.breakglass.tech/post/omegatech-bph-as202412-67-c2-servers-16-malware-families-one-subnet • https://www.spamhaus.org/sbl/listings/ghostynetworks.com
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes

let C2Domains = dynamic(["aryamint.com","scan.aryamint.com","talruit.com","mail.talruit.com","mpwirerope.com","ethara.org"]);
let C2Ports = dynamic([2002,2004,7273]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2Ips)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
   or (RemotePort in (C2Ports) and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

union isfuzzy=true

  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, SourceProcessName, DeviceVendor),
( DnsEvents

( ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr in (C2Ips) or DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or DstPortNumber in (C2Ports)
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url)

title: GHOSTYNETWORKS/OMEGATECH JS Backdoor C2 Indicators
id: 5c3a8f1e-7d2b-4e9a-9c4f-1a2b3c4d5e6f
description: Detects outbound traffic to Intrinsec-published C2 / spam-relay infrastructure for the March-April 2026 JS-backdoor campaign hosted on GHOSTYNETWORKS (AS205759) and OMEGATECH (AS202412), including the distinctive non-standard C2 ports 2002/2004/7273.
references:
  - https://www.intrinsec.com/en/pivoting-on-a-malspam-infrastructure-delivering-js-malware-backed-by-bulletproof-networks/
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-ghostynetworks-and-omegatech/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1571
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ip:
    DestinationIp:
      - '91.92.243.79'
      - '158.94.211.76'
      - '83.142.209.64'
  selection_domain:
    DestinationHostname:
      - 'aryamint.com'
      - 'scan.aryamint.com'
      - 'talruit.com'
      - 'mail.talruit.com'
      - 'mpwirerope.com'
      - 'ethara.org'
  selection_port_script:
    DestinationPort:
      - 2002
      - 2004
      - 7273
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
  condition: selection_ip or selection_domain or selection_port_script
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender OR firewall) (@DestinationIp:(91.92.243.79 OR 158.94.211.76 OR 83.142.209.64) OR @DestinationHostname:(aryamint.com OR scan.aryamint.com OR talruit.com OR mail.talruit.com OR mpwirerope.com OR ethara.org) OR (@DestinationPort:(2002 OR 2004 OR 7273) AND @Image:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe OR *\CSCRIPT.EXE OR *\mshta.exe OR *\MSHTA.EXE)))
#event_simpleName=/^(NetworkConnectIP4|NetworkConnectIP6|DnsRequest)$/
| case {
    #event_simpleName=DnsRequest | DomainName=/^(scan\.)?aryamint\.com$|^(mail\.)?talruit\.com$|^mpwirerope\.com$|^ethara\.org$/i ;
    #event_simpleName=/^NetworkConnectIP/ RemoteAddressIP4=/^(91\.92\.243\.79|158\.94\.211\.76|83\.142\.209\.64)$/ ;
    #event_simpleName=/^NetworkConnectIP/ RemotePort=/^(2002|2004|7273)$/ ContextImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript|mshta)\.exe$/i
}

[LLM] wscript/cscript executing .js extracted from archive utility (WinRAR/7zip/Explorer ZIP) Installation High
Article-specific delivery chain: phishing ZIP/RAR is opened, the embedded QUOTE_*.js / PO*.js is run via Windows Script Host. Detects script-host execution where the parent is an archive utility OR the JS file lives in a temp/extraction folder typical for archive-double-click handling. Pivots on the Intrinsec-named filenames and known SHA256 hashes. Rationale: Article-specific delivery chain (ZIP/RAR phishing → wscript/cscript → .js backdoor) anchored on the published filenames (QUOTE_B0426, PO 03603, PO 26683, PO8767), the five SHA256 hashes Intrinsec released, AND the extraction-folder fingerprints (`\AppData\Local\Temp\Rar$`, `\7z`, Outlook cache). Archive-parent → WSH child is a strong combination on its own; adding the campaign strings makes it alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.intrinsec.com/en/pivoting-on-a-malspam-infrastructure-delivering-js-malware-backed-by-bulletproof-networks/

[LLM] JS backdoor C2 traffic with outdated MSIE user-agent on non-standard ports Command & Control Medium
Article notes the backdoor disguises traffic with an outdated Internet Explorer user-agent over ports 2002/2004/7273 — an unusual combination because legitimate IE is end-of-life and almost never appears on those ports. Hunts proxy/firewall logs for MSIE-flavoured UAs egressing on the campaign's three ports, optionally tied to the IOC IPs. Rationale: Outdated `MSIE`/`Trident` UA + ports 2002/2004/7273 is a tight combination — the Intrinsec write-up calls this out specifically as the backdoor's traffic-disguise pattern. IE is EOL and largely absent from corporate egress, so a script host emitting that UA on a non-HTTP port is high-signal even without IP match. Sigma omitted because the cleanest version requires multi-table correlation (UA + port + script-host parent). Cross-checked against: • https://www.intrinsec.com/en/pivoting-on-a-malspam-infrastructure-delivering-js-malware-backed-by-bulletproof-networks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036 T1571
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

let C2Ips = dynamic(["91.92.243.79","158.94.211.76","83.142.209.64"]);
let C2Domains = dynamic(["aryamint.com","scan.aryamint.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
   and (RemotePort in (C2Ports) or RemoteIP in (C2Ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains))
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            DistDsts=dcount(RemoteIP), DistPorts=dcount_if(RemotePort, RemotePort in (C2Ports)),
            Hosts=make_set(DeviceName, 100), DstIps=make_set(RemoteIP, 50), DstUrls=make_set(RemoteUrl, 50)
            by InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where Connections >= 3 or DistPorts >= 1
| order by LastSeen desc

[LLM] Inbound email with ZIP/RAR attachment matching JS backdoor hashes or campaign filename pattern Delivery High
Front-of-funnel detection on the delivery vector: Intrinsec lists five SHA256 hashes (ZIP/RAR archives + the inner .js files) and a clear filename convention (QUOTE_*, PO*). Hits EmailAttachmentInfo for any of those exact hashes or the filename pattern with .zip/.rar/.js/.jse/.mjs extensions, so we can pull recipient lists before the user double-clicks. Rationale: Pre-execution choke point: any of the five exact SHA256 hashes from the Intrinsec IOC table, the campaign's filename regex `(QUOTE_B0426|PO_xxxx|PO8767).(js|jse|mjs|zip|rar)`, the spam-emitting domains (talruit.com, mpwirerope.com, ethara.org), or the two spam-relay IPs (83.142.209.64, 91.92.243.79). Hash match is single-source from Intrinsec, but a SHA256 is unambiguous — zero collision risk. Cross-checked against: • https://www.intrinsec.com/en/pivoting-on-a-malspam-infrastructure-delivering-js-malware-backed-by-bulletproof-networks/ • https://intel.breakglass.tech/post/omegatech-bph-as202412-67-c2-servers-16-malware-families-one-subnet

EmailAttachmentInfo

| extend SpamInfraMatch = SenderMailFromDomain in~ (SpamDomains) or SenderIPv4 in (SenderIps)
| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("794fab796e48f97e976d99157913ab5beee5ae8ef2731bf2af2222ae5b6a1c65", "ac842e4adb445a76aad135828d56116858a1b7d37b4a103f493e175816df9bb2", "33713a3650a3c1d64045c3832835dcacef92ad4f09c030fbe674454266880fea", "7277f4dfb26a53f8ee47cac051a82f6709e07b6603f26ff3987cc64a137e07dc", "232a179daf4db527c062b609ebb5f19310eea8f5c80afce6f763f5841110aed8") or SHA1 in~ ("794fab796e48f97e976d99157913ab5beee5ae8ef2731bf2af2222ae5b6a1c65", "ac842e4adb445a76aad135828d56116858a1b7d37b4a103f493e175816df9bb2", "33713a3650a3c1d64045c3832835dcacef92ad4f09c030fbe674454266880fea", "7277f4dfb26a53f8ee47cac051a82f6709e07b6603f26ff3987cc64a137e07dc", "232a179daf4db527c062b609ebb5f19310eea8f5c80afce6f763f5841110aed8") or MD5 in~ ("794fab796e48f97e976d99157913ab5beee5ae8ef2731bf2af2222ae5b6a1c65", "ac842e4adb445a76aad135828d56116858a1b7d37b4a103f493e175816df9bb2", "33713a3650a3c1d64045c3832835dcacef92ad4f09c030fbe674454266880fea", "7277f4dfb26a53f8ee47cac051a82f6709e07b6603f26ff3987cc64a137e07dc", "232a179daf4db527c062b609ebb5f19310eea8f5c80afce6f763f5841110aed8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("794fab796e48f97e976d99157913ab5beee5ae8ef2731bf2af2222ae5b6a1c65", "ac842e4adb445a76aad135828d56116858a1b7d37b4a103f493e175816df9bb2", "33713a3650a3c1d64045c3832835dcacef92ad4f09c030fbe674454266880fea", "7277f4dfb26a53f8ee47cac051a82f6709e07b6603f26ff3987cc64a137e07dc", "232a179daf4db527c062b609ebb5f19310eea8f5c80afce6f763f5841110aed8") or SHA1 in~ ("794fab796e48f97e976d99157913ab5beee5ae8ef2731bf2af2222ae5b6a1c65", "ac842e4adb445a76aad135828d56116858a1b7d37b4a103f493e175816df9bb2", "33713a3650a3c1d64045c3832835dcacef92ad4f09c030fbe674454266880fea", "7277f4dfb26a53f8ee47cac051a82f6709e07b6603f26ff3987cc64a137e07dc", "232a179daf4db527c062b609ebb5f19310eea8f5c80afce6f763f5841110aed8") or MD5 in~ ("794fab796e48f97e976d99157913ab5beee5ae8ef2731bf2af2222ae5b6a1c65", "ac842e4adb445a76aad135828d56116858a1b7d37b4a103f493e175816df9bb2", "33713a3650a3c1d64045c3832835dcacef92ad4f09c030fbe674454266880fea", "7277f4dfb26a53f8ee47cac051a82f6709e07b6603f26ff3987cc64a137e07dc", "232a179daf4db527c062b609ebb5f19310eea8f5c80afce6f763f5841110aed8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["794fab796e48f97e976d99157913ab5beee5ae8ef2731bf2af2222ae5b6a1c65", "ac842e4adb445a76aad135828d56116858a1b7d37b4a103f493e175816df9bb2", "33713a3650a3c1d64045c3832835dcacef92ad4f09c030fbe674454266880fea", "7277f4dfb26a53f8ee47cac051a82f6709e07b6603f26ff3987cc64a137e07dc", "232a179daf4db527c062b609ebb5f19310eea8f5c80afce6f763f5841110aed8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Purchase-order phishing delivering pankocrs.js JavaScript loader Delivery High
Hunts inbound emails carrying the PureLogs JavaScript loader (pankocrs.js or similar .js inside archive) with purchase-order lures, plus the subsequent .js drop to disk by an archiver. Article-specific because it anchors on the named filename and the PO/invoice subject pattern. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact attachment name (pankocrs.js) and the explicitly stated purchase-order theme. Cross-checked Fortinet's prior PureLogs reporting on cybersecuritynews.com and the campaign's stated lure pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-purelogs-variant-uses-msbuild-exe-process-hollowing/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
let lures = dynamic(["purchase order","purchase-order","invoice","quotation","PO#","order confirmation"]);
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "pankocrs.js" or (FileName endswith ".js" and FileType in~ ("js","javascript","zip","rar","7z"))
| join kind=inner (EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d)) on NetworkMessageId
| where FileName =~ "pankocrs.js" or Subject has_any (lures)
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, SHA256, DeliveryAction
| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] wscript/cscript spawning PowerShell that loads .NET assembly (PureLogs stage 2) Installation High
Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe executing a .js (e.g. pankocrs.js) and spawning powershell.exe whose script body contains [Reflection.Assembly]::Load / Invoke-AssemblyMethod / IEX patterns consistent with the PureLogs in-memory .NET loader. Rationale: Pairs the named .js entry-vector (pankocrs.js / ps_qnSEGUkU0LIY*.ps1) with the article's explicit Invoke-AssemblyMethod / Invoke-Expression in-memory .NET load. Cross-checked MITRE T1620 (Reflective Code Loading) and the kill-chain log_sources list. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001 T1620

| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pankocrs.js",".js")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Reflection.Assembly","Invoke-AssemblyMethod","IEX","Invoke-Expression","FromBase64String","ps_qnSEGUkU0LIY")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Reflection.Assembly","Invoke-AssemblyMethod","IEX","Invoke-Expression","FromBase64String","ps_qnSEGUkU0LIY",".js")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PowerShell launching MsBuild.exe with no project file (PureLogs hollowing target) Installation High
Detects powershell.exe spawning msbuild.exe with no .csproj / .sln / .xml argument — the precondition for the PureLogs downloader to hollow MsBuild and inject the stealer. Article-specific because MsBuild abuse here originates from the JS->PowerShell chain, not from a real build environment. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit chain: powershell.exe -> msbuild.exe used as a hollow target. Filtering out project-file args removes legitimate developer builds, which is the core FP source for T1218.014. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/014/ • https://lolbas-project.github.io/lolbas/Binaries/Msbuild/
ATT&CKT1218.014 T1055.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "msbuild.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (".csproj",".sln",".vbproj",".proj",".targets",".xml"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\MSBuild.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| where not (CommandLine has_any (".csproj",".sln",".vbproj",".proj",".targets",".xml"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cross-process injection (CreateRemoteThread / WriteProcessMemory) targeting MsBuild.exe Installation High
Hunts cross-process memory writes and remote thread creations where the target image is MsBuild.exe and the injector is not a known development tool — the exact PureLogs hollowing primitive described in the article (CreateProcessA + WriteProcessMemory + ResumeThread). Rationale: Targets the three Win32 calls (CreateProcessA / WriteProcessMemory / ResumeThread) named verbatim in the article's hollowing description. Filtering known dev-tool injectors (devenv/dotnet/VBCSCompiler) eliminates the dominant FP class. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("devenv.exe","dotnet.exe","VBCSCompiler.exe","MSBuild.exe")

| ContextImageFileName!=/(devenv|dotnet|VBCSCompiler|MSBuild)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetImageFileName], function=count())

[LLM] MsBuild.exe reading browser Login Data / wallet / mail credential stores Actions on Objectives High
Detects MsBuild.exe (which should never touch user credential stores) opening browser Login Data SQLite files, crypto wallet directories, Thunderbird/Outlook/Foxmail profiles, FileZilla recentservers.xml, or OpenVPN/ProtonVPN config dirs — the post-injection credential-harvest behaviour of PureLogs. Rationale: The article explicitly names the %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\Login Data path and the full list of targeted apps (Exodus, Electrum, Atomic, Thunderbird, Foxmail, FileZilla, OpenVPN, ProtonVPN). MsBuild.exe has zero legitimate reason to touch these stores, making this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/ • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1138/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1552.001

[LLM] MsBuild.exe HTTPS C2 beacon to 77.83.39.211 (PureLogs exfil) Command & Control High
Detects outbound HTTPS connections from msbuild.exe to the article's stated C2 IP 77.83.39.211, or any public IP from msbuild.exe (which has no legitimate reason to beacon). Pairs the named IOC with the post-hollowing exfil path. Rationale: Anchors on the article's pre-extracted C2 IP 77.83.39.211 paired with msbuild.exe as the originating process. Cross-checked the IP against AbuseIPDB pattern and the article's HttpClient.GetAsync() C2 method. MSBuild as a network originator is itself unusual enough to alert on even without the IP match. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.002 T1041

| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteIP == "77.83.39.211" or RemotePort in (443, 80, 8080, 8443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SourceProcessName endswith "MSBuild.exe" or DeviceCustomString1 endswith "MSBuild.exe"
| where DestinationIP == "77.83.39.211" or RequestURL has "77.83.39.211"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceProcessName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
