Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

[LLM] Post-takedown beacon to CrowdStrike Glassworm sinkhole 164.92.88.210 Command & Control High
Hunts any outbound connection from a developer endpoint to CrowdStrike's announced sinkhole IP 164.92.88.210. Per the article, every still-infected Glassworm host beacons to this address post-disruption, making it a near-zero-FP confirmed-infection indicator. Rationale: 164.92.88.210 is CrowdStrike's named sinkhole — the article explicitly says all still-infected machines now beacon here, making any hit a confirmed legacy Glassworm infection. Cross-checked CrowdStrike's own write-up referenced in the article and the Shadowserver Foundation sinkhole pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/ • https://www.shadowserver.org/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "164.92.88.210"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "164.92.88.210" or SourceIP == "164.92.88.210"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound connection to Glassworm operator VPS C2 infrastructure Command & Control High
Hunts outbound connections from any endpoint to the four operator-controlled VPS IPs Glassworm used for direct C2 / payload delivery. These remain valuable because retrospective searches reveal which dev workstations were infected before the takedown. Rationale: These four IPs are listed in the article's pre-extracted IOC block as the direct-server C2 layer beneath the Solana/BitTorrent/Calendar resolution dance. Exact-match IP hunting is the highest-fidelity pivot available against Glassworm. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/ • https://www.shadowserver.org/

[LLM] VS Code / Node / Cursor process resolving Solana mainnet RPC (Glassworm C2 channel) Command & Control Medium
Hunts developer-IDE / node processes resolving or connecting to api.mainnet-beta.solana.com and other Solana RPC endpoints — the article describes GlasswormRAT pulling C2 addresses from Solana memo fields. Legitimate Solana RPC traffic from a non-wallet, non-blockchain-dev workstation is anomalous. Rationale: The article explicitly names Solana blockchain memos as one of the four resolution layers; api.mainnet-beta.solana.com is the default Solana RPC endpoint. Limiting parent-process to dev IDEs (Code.exe / node.exe / cursor.exe / electron.exe) keeps the FP rate sane because real Solana developers do exist. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.solana.com/cluster/rpc-endpoints • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/001/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("mainnet-beta.solana.com", "solana-api.projectserum.com", "api.devnet.solana.com", "rpc.ankr.com/solana", ".solana.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","node.exe","cursor.exe","code - insiders.exe","electron.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let SolanaHosts = dynamic(["api.mainnet-beta.solana.com","solana-api.projectserum.com","api.devnet.solana.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (SolanaHosts) or Name endswith ".solana.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/glassworm-botnet-disrupted-after-resilient-c2-infrastructure-takedown/
author: SOC Detection Engineering

detection:

      - '\node.exe'
      - '\Cursor.exe'
      - '\electron.exe'
  selection_dest:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'mainnet-beta.solana.com'
      - 'solana-api.projectserum.com'
      - '.solana.com'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_dest
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\Code.exe OR *\code.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\Cursor.exe OR *\electron.exe)) (@DestinationHostname:(*mainnet-beta.solana.com* OR *solana-api.projectserum.com* OR *.solana.com))

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

[LLM] Developer endpoint emitting BitTorrent DHT bootstrap traffic from non-torrent process Command & Control High
Hunts for UDP traffic to BitTorrent DHT bootstrap nodes (router.bittorrent.com, dht.transmissionbt.com, router.utorrent.com) originating from VS Code / Node / Cursor processes. The article names BitTorrent DHT as one of Glassworm's four C2 resolution channels — legitimate developer workstations should never have an IDE process querying the DHT. Rationale: BitTorrent DHT is the second of Glassworm's four C2 channels per the article. DHT traffic from a code-editor process tree is extremely abnormal — torrent clients run as their own binaries, never embedded inside VS Code. Cross-checked the BitTorrent DHT BEP-0005 bootstrap routers list. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0005.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/002/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let DhtBootstrap = dynamic(["router.bittorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","router.utorrent.com","dht.libtorrent.org","router.silotis.us"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","node.exe","cursor.exe","electron.exe","code - insiders.exe")
| where (RemoteUrl has_any (DhtBootstrap)) or (Protocol == "Udp" and RemotePort between (6881 .. 6889))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let DhtBootstrap = dynamic(["router.bittorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","router.utorrent.com","dht.libtorrent.org"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (DhtBootstrap)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IDE Process Querying BitTorrent DHT (Glassworm C2 Channel)

[LLM] IDE / Node process resolving calendar.google.com as Glassworm C2 dead-drop Command & Control Medium
Hunts for non-browser developer-tool processes (Code.exe, node.exe, cursor.exe, electron.exe) making DNS or HTTPS calls to calendar.google.com / googleapis.com calendar endpoints. Glassworm uses Google Calendar event titles as Base64-encoded C2 dead-drop locations — legitimate IDEs do not hit the Calendar API. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'Glassworm uses Google Calendar event titles as dead-drop locations for Base64-encoded C2 paths'. Scoping the parent process to VS Code / Node keeps FP rate manageable since legitimate calendar use happens in browsers, not IDEs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/001/ • https://developers.google.com/calendar/api/v3/reference
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","node.exe","cursor.exe","electron.exe","code - insiders.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("calendar.google.com", "www.googleapis.com/calendar", "clients6.google.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let CalendarHosts = dynamic(["calendar.google.com","www.googleapis.com","clients6.google.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (CalendarHosts)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IDE Process Querying Google Calendar (Glassworm Dead Drop)

[LLM] Trojanized Glassworm VS Code / OpenVSX extension package files on developer host Installation High
Hunts for file-write events under %USERPROFILE%\.vscode\extensions or ~/.vscode-server matching the eight Glassworm-trojanized extension package names. Any installation directory containing these is a confirmed compromise indicator regardless of network telemetry. Rationale: The kill-chain block enumerates exactly eight package names as Glassworm IOCs. Any file write under .vscode/extensions matching one of these is a confirmed install of a trojanized package — there is no benign overlap with these specific names. Confirmed via CrowdStrike's disclosure referenced in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/ • https://open-vsx.org/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1176 T1546.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let GlasswormPkgs = dynamic(["codejoy-vscode-extension","vscode-theme-seti-folder","serenity-dsl-syntaxhighlight","rust-doc-viewer","dark-theme-sm","git-worktree-menu","better-nunjucks","recoil"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.vscode\extensions\", "/.vscode-server/extensions/", "/.vscode/extensions/")
| where FolderPath has_any (GlasswormPkgs) or FileName has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let GlasswormPkgs = dynamic(["codejoy-vscode-extension","vscode-theme-seti-folder","serenity-dsl-syntaxhighlight","rust-doc-viewer","dark-theme-sm","git-worktree-menu","better-nunjucks","recoil"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.vscode\extensions\", "/.vscode-server/extensions/", "/.vscode/extensions/")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] VS Code child process reads wallet / dev-credential files (Glassworm credential theft) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for Code.exe / node.exe / electron.exe (or their child processes) reading high-value credential or wallet files within seconds of an extension directory write — the article describes trojanized extensions harvesting cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials. Rationale: Article: 'stole cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials'. Combines the IDE-process predicate (Glassworm runs inside the extension host) with the canonical credential / wallet file paths — both halves are documented in the article's kill-chain block. MetaMask extension ID nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn corroborated from Chrome Web Store. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/ • https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/metamask/nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn
ATT&CKT1555 T1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
let CredTargets = dynamic([
    @"\.aws\credentials", @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"\.ssh\id_ed25519", @"\.npmrc", @"\.git-credentials",
    @"\Local Extension Settings\nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn", // MetaMask
    @"\Local Extension Settings\ejbalbakoplchlghecdalmeeeajnimhm", // MetaMask (Edge)
    "wallet.dat", @"\Exodus\exodus.wallet", @"\Electrum\wallets"
]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileOpened","FileRead","FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","node.exe","electron.exe","cursor.exe","code - insiders.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredTargets) or FileName has_any (CredTargets)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let CredTargets = dynamic([@"\.aws\credentials", @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"\.ssh\id_ed25519", @"\.npmrc", @"\.git-credentials", @"\Local Extension Settings\nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn", "wallet.dat", @"\Exodus\exodus.wallet", @"\Electrum\wallets"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("code.exe","node.exe","electron.exe","cursor.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredTargets)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] First-time install of any Glassworm-named extension across the org (baseline anti-join) Delivery Medium
Surfaces the first organisation-wide installation of any of the eight named Glassworm extension package names. Defenders who haven't yet hit Glassworm get an early-warning signal as soon as a developer pulls a re-uploaded clone. Designed for environments where IOC names may resurface under typosquatted variants. Rationale: The eight package names are explicit Glassworm IOCs from the kill-chain block. Baseline anti-join means SOC only sees a host the *first* time it picks up a trojanized extension — avoids alert fatigue once a host is already known-compromised. Sigma omitted because anti-join over baseline is a correlation, not single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://open-vsx.org/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let GlasswormPkgs = dynamic(["codejoy-vscode-extension","vscode-theme-seti-folder","serenity-dsl-syntaxhighlight","rust-doc-viewer","dark-theme-sm","git-worktree-menu","better-nunjucks","recoil"]);
let Baseline = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where FolderPath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
    | where FolderPath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
    | summarize by DeviceName;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
| where FolderPath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), arg_min(Timestamp, *) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| project FirstSeen, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by FirstSeen desc
let GlasswormPkgs = dynamic(["codejoy-vscode-extension","vscode-theme-seti-folder","serenity-dsl-syntaxhighlight","rust-doc-viewer","dark-theme-sm","git-worktree-menu","better-nunjucks","recoil"]);
let Baseline = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
    | where TargetFilePath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
    | summarize by DvcHostname;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DvcHostname
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), arg_min(TimeGenerated, *) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),

| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted IT-helpdesk lookalike domain resolution · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted IT-helpdesk lookalike domain resolution Delivery High
Surfaces DNS resolution or HTTP traffic from any corporate endpoint to the SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted helpdesk lookalike domains named in the May 2026 FBI flash alert. Catches the lure infrastructure used to coach employees into calling fake IT support. Rationale: Domains pulled verbatim from the article IOC list (duanemorris-helpdesk.com, perkinscoie-helpdesk.com, millermartin-helpdesk.com). EclecticIQ May 2025 report and the May 2025 FBI PIN both confirm Luna Moth's pattern of registering law-firm-themed helpdesk lookalikes, so the typosquat shape is corroborated. [LLM] SRG in-person USB exfil: mass file copy to non-system drive after remote-help tool Actions on Objectives Medium
Catches the SRG fallback playbook — when the phone-based remote-desktop attempt fails, an SRG operative shows up in person and copies data via USB/external HDD. Looks for a burst of file writes to a non-C: drive shortly after a known remote-help binary executed on the same host. Rationale: Article explicitly states: 'SRG sends a threat actor to the victim's location to gain access to insert a storage device into the victim's computer' and 'steal data by connecting USB drives or external hard drives'. The remote-help tool list comes from EclecticIQ + prior FBI PIN documentation of Luna Moth's preferred RMM tooling (Zoho Assist, AnyDesk, Splashtop, Atera, Syncro). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/luna-moth-callback-phishing-campaign-targets-us-legal-and-financial-firms • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-silent-ransom-group-targets-law-firms-in-callback-phishing-attacks/

let RecentRemoteHelp = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (RemoteHelpTools)
    | project RemoteHelpTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteHelpTool = FileName;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")

| where FileCount > 200

| where FirstWrite between (RemoteHelpTime .. RemoteHelpTime + 6h)
| project FirstWrite, LastWrite, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteHelpTool, RemoteHelpTime, FileCount, TotalBytes, Drives, SampleFiles
| order by FileCount desc

[LLM] SRG extortion leak-site contact: traffic to business-data-leaks.com Actions on Objectives High
Detects any outbound contact from a corporate endpoint to the SRG/Luna Moth public leak site business-data-leaks.com. A hit means either a victim navigating to verify a ransom threat, or an SRG-controlled host inside the network signalling/posting. Rationale: business-data-leaks.com is named in the article as the SRG-controlled leak site used to extort victims. Any outbound hit from a corp host is presumptively malicious or victim-impact-stage — extremely low base rate. Cross-checked with the May 2025 FBI PIN and EclecticIQ writeup which both reference Luna Moth's data-leak-site model. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/luna-moth-callback-phishing-campaign-targets-us-legal-and-financial-firms • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-silent-ransom-group-targets-law-firms-in-callback-phishing-attacks/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"

status: experimental

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("business-data-leaks.com", "duanemorris-helpdesk.com", "perkinscoie-helpdesk.com", "millermartin-helpdesk.com", "kobrekim-helpdesk.com", "ciso-helpdesk.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["business-data-leaks.com", "duanemorris-helpdesk.com", "perkinscoie-helpdesk.com", "millermartin-helpdesk.com", "kobrekim-helpdesk.com", "ciso-helpdesk.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:

    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:

    selection_domain:
